plan.contextChunk: This figure is a shaded perspective drawing of a clear cylindrical container partly filled with a pale blue liquid. The vessel has an elliptical rim with a thick rounded glass lip, a slightly darker band marking the liquid surface a short way down, and a darker pooled region across the curved bottom. Three small cubes outlined in black dashed lines sit at different places within the liquid, each drawn in the container's perspective and each carrying a numeral: cube 1 high and toward the left, cube 2 a little lower and to the right, and cube 3 near the bottom center. A curved arrow links each cube to its own label, written as a ratio in tall parentheses with a subscript, reading Δm/ΔV with subscript 1 at the upper right, Δm/ΔV with subscript 2 at the middle right, and Δm/ΔV with subscript 3 out to the left. Giving each sampling cube its own subscripted mass-to-volume ratio invites the reader to treat the three as separate numbers rather than one value for the whole vessel, which is how local density is defined point by point.

elliptical liquid free-surface a short way below the rim (slightly darker band)

interactions.label: Sample volume edge L
interactions.teaches: Shrinking the cube reduces both Δm and ΔV, but their ratio converges to a single point value — local density is the limit of Δm/ΔV as the surrounding volume becomes small

interactions.label: Fluid
interactions.teaches: In a uniform fluid all three sampled ratios are equal (one bulk density); in a heterogeneous fluid they differ by position, making the contrast between a single bulk density and a position-dependent local density visible

demo_steps.title: Uniform fluid, default cube
demo_steps.narration: With a uniform liquid, click any cube — its Δm/ΔV equals the same bulk density ρ₀ no matter which point you sample.

demo_steps.title: Heterogeneous fluid
demo_steps.narration: Switch to a heterogeneous liquid (density increasing with depth). Now cube 3 near the bottom gives a larger Δm/ΔV than cube 1 near the surface — density depends on position.

demo_steps.title: Shrink the sample volume
demo_steps.narration: Drag the edge length down. Δm and ΔV both shrink, yet the ratio at the selected cube settles toward the local point density, illustrating the limiting definition ρ = lim Δm/ΔV.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: cylinder radius R≈1.2, height H≈3.0, axis vertical (Y), base at y=0, rim at y=3.0. Liquid fills to y≈2.1 (free-surface ellipse there); a darker pooled cap shades y∈[0,0.35]. Glass wall = open CylinderGeometry (no caps) radius 1.2, height 3.0, color #cfeef0 opacity ~0.18; rim = TorusGeometry radius 1.2 tube 0.09 at y=3.0 color #d8f1f2. Liquid = CylinderGeometry radius 1.16 height 2.1 centered y=1.05 color #bcd6ee opacity ~0.5; surface band = thin cylinder ring at y=2.1 color #a9c8e6; bottom pool = short cylinder y∈[0,0.35] color #8fb4d8 opacity 0.6. Sample cubes (edge L, default 0.45) drawn as 12 dashed black edges (LineDashedMaterial, dashSize 0.06 gap 0.04) plus a centered numeral sprite: cube1 center (-0.45,1.7,0.15), cube2 center (0.5,1.25,0.1), cube3 center (0.0,0.5,0.25) — matching high-left / mid-right / bottom-center. Curved arrows = QuadraticBezierCurve3 from a cube face to its label anchor, black, with a small cone arrowhead. Label anchors: (Δm/ΔV)₁ at (2.1,2.0,0), (Δm/ΔV)₂ at (2.1,1.2,0), (Δm/ΔV)₃ at (-2.3,0.7,0). Density model: uniform ρ=ρ₀=1000 kg/m³; heterogeneous ρ(y)=ρ₀+κ·(2.1−y) with κ≈250 kg/m³ per unit height (deeper→denser). Displayed ratio = ρ(local at cube center) + ε·(L/Lmax)·spread so a large cube averages over the gradient (extra deviation) and shrinking drives it to the point value; ΔV=L³, Δm=ratio·ΔV. Selected cube highlight = solid orange #ff8800 edges + faint orange fill opacity 0.15. Palette: glass #cfeef0, liquid #bcd6ee, surface #a9c8e6, pool #8fb4d8, dashes/labels #111111, highlight #ff8800.
interactionPlan.notes: Render dashed cube edges with THREE.LineDashedMaterial and call computeLineDistances() on each Line; rebuild edge geometry when the sampleSize slider changes. Ratio labels and the live readout are canvas-texture Sprites regenerated on every click/slider/toggle change. Keep both fluid models' ratio values computed on the fly; the toggle only switches which ρ field feeds the readouts and recolors the liquid slightly (uniform flat tint vs a vertical gradient shader/vertexColors for heterogeneous). Arrows and labels live outside the glass so they stay legible; disable raycasting on arrows/labels so only the three cubes are clickable. Use a subtle vertical gradient (vertex colors darker at the bottom) for the heterogeneous liquid to visually cue the depth-dependent density.

authoredContext:
The density of a substance is not necessarily constant throughout the volume of a substance. If the density is constant throughout a substance, the substance is said to be a homogeneous substance. A solid iron bar is an example of a homogeneous substance. The density is constant throughout, and the density of any sample of the substance is the same as its average density. If the density of a substance were not constant, the substance is said to be a heterogeneous substance. A chunk of Swiss cheese is an example of a heterogeneous material containing both the solid cheese and gas-filled voids. The density at a specific location within a heterogeneous material is called local density, and is given as a function of location, ρ=ρ(x,y,z) (the figure).

Density may vary throughout a heterogeneous mixture. Local density at a point is obtained from dividing mass by volume in a small volume around a given point.

Figure is a drawing of a container filled with a liquid. Small cubes are drawn in different regions of the container to indicate local density points.

Local density can be obtained by a limiting process, based on the average density in a small volume around the point in question, taking the limit where the size of the volume approaches zero,
